ABSTRACT Introduction Although an acute exercise session typically increases bone turnover markers (BTM), the impact of subsequent sessions and the interaction with preexercise calcium intake remain unclear despite the application to the “real-life” training of many competitive athletes. Methods Using a randomized crossover design, elite male rowers ( n = 16) completed two trials, a week apart, consisting of two 90-min rowing ergometer sessions (EX1, EX2) separated by 150 min. Before each trial, participants consumed a high (CAL; ~1000 mg) or isocaloric low (CON; <10 mg) calcium meal. Biochemical markers including parathyroid hormone (PTH), serum ionized calcium (iCa) and BTMs (C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen, osteocalcin) were monitored from baseline to 3 h after EX2. Results Although each session caused perturbances of serum iCa, CAL maintained calcium concentrations above those of CON for most time points, 4.5% and 2.4% higher after EX1 and EX2, respectively. The decrease in iCa in CON was associated with an elevation of blood PTH ( P < 0.05) and C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen ( P < 0.0001) over this period of repeated training sessions and their recovery, particularly during and after EX2. Preexercise intake of calcium-rich foods lowered BTM over the course of a day with several training sessions. Conclusions Preexercise intake of a calcium-rich meal before training sessions undertaken within the same day had a cumulative and prolonged effect on the stabilization of blood iCa during exercise. In turn, this reduced the postexercise PTH response, potentially attenuating the increase in markers of bone resorption. Such practical strategies may be integrated into the athlete’s overall sports nutrition plan, with the potential to safeguard long-term bone health and reduce the risk of bone stress injuries. Key Words ENDURANCE NUTRIENT TIMING OSTEOCALCIN PTH Β-CTX-I CALCIUM BONE OPEN-ACCESS TRUE Athletes often exhibit suboptimal bone health despite the well-known positive effects of exercise on bone ( 1 ). Immediate concerns include the effects of bone stress injuries on training consistency and availability for competition, whereas an increased risk of osteoporosis-related fractures may be seen later in an athlete’s career or after retirement ( 2 , 3 ). Such issues are known in a variety of sports such as cycling ( 4 ), dance ( 5 ), and distance running ( 6 ) and are seen among males and females ( 7 ). Key contributors toward bone health include energy availability, weight-bearing/bone loading exercise, and vitamin D ( 1 , 8 ). However, some athletes do consistently optimize these factors, and/or they may still require other measures to adequately support bone health. Therefore, there is interest in addressing other mechanisms by which bone metabolism may be perturbed. Elite rowers typically present with normal areal bone mineral density (aBMD) relative to general population norms; however, this may be inadequate to withstand the load required by the sport ( 9 ) and may be associated with history of bone stress injury of the rib ( 10 ), associated with significant training time loss and performance decrement ( 11 ). A series of studies have identified that acute changes in serum ionized calcium (iCa) was associated with exercise correlate with bone turnover. For example, 2 h of moderate-intensity cycling in male cyclists was associated with a decrease in iCa and an elevation in parathyroid hormone (PTH) ( 12 ), suggesting that bone resorption may have been upregulated in an attempt to stabilize the reduction in iCa. It was hypothesized that increasing absorption of calcium from the gut during exercise, achieved by consuming calcium-rich foods or supplements before or during the session, might prevent bone resorption by providing an alternative calcium source. Indeed, preexercise calcium intake in elite male triathletes ( 13 ), as well as male ( 14 ) and female ( 15 ) cyclists, was found to suppress the cycling-associated rise in PTH and attenuated the increase in C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (β-CTX-1), a marker of bone breakdown, in some ( 13 , 15 ), but not all, protocols ( 14 ). The divergent outcomes may be due to differences in the source and timing of calcium intake (>60 vs 20 min prior). Studies in older individuals with lower levels of fitness who undertook brisk walking exercise also show similar responses to calcium support ( 16 – 18 ). These studies provide robust evidence that exercise disrupts calcium homeostasis, likely triggered by a decline in iCa and resulting in an increase in PTH and β-CTX-I. The cause of the perturbation of iCa during exercise and whether this contributes to chronic and clinically meaningful changes in aBMD are still to be determined ( 19 ). The original hypothesis of dermal (sweat) mineral losses ( 20 ) was disproven in two different models. In young adults, there was no difference in exercise-associated iCa changes when brisk walking was undertaken in cool or warm conditions, despite differences in sweat/calcium losses. A more sophisticated methodology, involving the use of an intravenous calcium clamp to maintain iCa allowed more frequent blood sampling, including midexercise samples. Here, a drop in iCa was observed within the first 15 min of a 60-min cycling session at 80% heart rate (HR) maximum, well before significant sweat loss, with the calcium infusion attenuating the increase in PTH and CTX compared with the saline control ( 21 ). Phosphate has also been investigated given its involvement with PTH control at rest and exercise recovery; however, iCa seems more tightly linked with exercise-related PTH changes ( 22 ). To date, studies of these perturbations in iCa and bone metabolism have focused on a single exercise session. However, high-performance athletes typically train multiple times a day, with subsequent sessions frequently commencing within 2–3 h, or before bone responses to the first session have normalized ( 15 ). The acute bone response to repeated exercise sessions has been briefly studied. Scott et al. ( 23 ) investigated the effect of the recovery period (3 vs 23 h) between two bouts of running on bone metabolism, before and during exercise on the trial days and for the following 4 d. Reducing the recovery time from 23 to 3 h did not alter the iCa, PTH, or β-CTX-I response to the second exercise bout or affect P1NP, a marker of bone formation that generally has a more chronic response to stimulus. In contrast, a very short recovery window (40 min) showed a blunting of the PTH response by the rest period ( 24 ). The response to preexercise calcium over multiple sessions has not yet been examined. Together, these studies indicate a perturbation in bone turnover in response to exercise, likely triggered by a decline in iCa, resulting in a PTH-mediated increase in bone resorption. It occurs in a range of ages and fitness levels, between sexes, and in different modes and intensities of exercise. Preexercise calcium intake may maintain iCa and attenuate markers of bone resorption during and after the exercise session. Given the importance of deciphering the real-life significance of preexercise calcium supplementation, this study examined the effect of multiple sessions of exercise in a day (i.e., a typical training day for a high-performance athlete) bone turnover marker (BTM) in elite male rowers, using dietary opportunities to provide preexercise calcium supplementation.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Acute exercise sessions; Repeated strenuous non-weight-bearing endurance exercise (e.g., rowing) involving two 90-min sessions separated by 150 min; High vs. low calcium dietary interventions.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Acute or repeated strenuous non-weight-bearing endurance exercise typically causes a perturbation and decline in serum ionized calcium (iCa) through an undetermined mechanism. This decrease triggers a homeostatic response involving an elevation of parathyroid hormone (PTH), which subsequently upregulates bone resorption, leading to an increase in C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (β-CTX-1), a marker of bone breakdown. Repeated exercise sessions without adequate calcium intake can prolong this state, favoring bone loss. Preexercise intake of a calcium-rich meal (e.g., ~1000 mg) provides an alternative calcium source, helping to stabilize blood iCa during exercise and reducing exercise-mediated blood calcium losses. This improved iCa maintenance attenuates the postexercise PTH response, thereby mitigating the increase in markers of bone resorption. Marginally elevated cortisol may also contribute to bone loss independently. Adjustment for hemoconcentration did not alter the interpretation of bone turnover markers, indicating true physiological changes rather than fluid shifts.
related_biomarkers: C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (β-CTX-1)

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study involved a randomized crossover design comparing a high calcium meal (~1000 mg or 1000-1200 mg) with an isocaloric low calcium meal (<10 mg calcium) consumed before training sessions. The high calcium meal, provided via dairy foods, was effective in maintaining iCa concentrations and significantly attenuating increases in PTH and β-CTX-1 during and after repeated strenuous exercise sessions, compared to the low calcium meal. Small differences in energy, protein, and fat intake between trials were noted but deemed clinically insignificant (~10 kJ·kg−1, 0.3 g·kg−1 protein, 0.1 g·kg−1 fat). Exercise intensity (mean power output) was not significantly different between the high and low calcium interventions (P = 0.27) or between sessions (P = 0.35). The optimal dose of preexercise calcium has not been identified.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The study specifically examined the impact of acute calcium intake during a 'real-life' training day involving multiple strenuous, non-weight-bearing exercise sessions (rowing) within the same day in elite male rowers. This context, with its focus on repeated sessions and non-weight-bearing activity, was not thoroughly examined previously. The dietary intervention was specific to countering the exercise-associated reduction in blood calcium. Findings on bone turnover markers (BTMs) were robust, as adjustment for hemoconcentration did not alter their interpretation, and sweat loss was accounted for as a covariate in β-CTX-I adj analysis, indicating true physiological changes not confounded by fluid shifts.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Elite male rowers (N=16), including world-class, international, and national level athletes, some of whom presented with low bone density (z < -1 for proximal femur) and insufficient 25(OH)D levels (<80 nmol·L−1). The findings are also broadly applicable to competitive athletes and high-performance athletes in sports involving repeated non-weight-bearing activity, such as lightweight rowers who are identified as a high-risk group for bone-related injuries.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Athletes often exhibit suboptimal bone health despite the positive effects of exercise, leading to immediate concerns like bone stress injuries (e.g., rib stress injuries in rowers) affecting training consistency and competition availability, and an increased risk of osteoporosis-related fractures later in their careers. Preexercise intake of a calcium-rich meal provides a protective benefit by stabilizing blood iCa, preventing increases in PTH, and mitigating the pronounced increase in bone resorption markers (e.g., β-CTX-1) during and after strenuous exercise. This strategy has the potential to safeguard long-term bone health, support calcium homeostasis, and reduce the risk of bone stress injuries, and can be integrated into an athlete's overall sports nutrition plan, addressing impairments of bone remodeling relevant to health and performance.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Suboptimal bone health and bone stress injuries represent an adverse risk for athletes due to prolonged periods favoring bone resorption, compromised areal bone mineral density (aBMD), and a high burden of injuries. Preexercise calcium intake offers a protective benefit by mitigating these adverse effects, supporting bone health, and attenuating exercise-induced bone resorption.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study indicates that systemic markers of bone turnover, specifically iCa, PTH, and β-CTX-1, reliably show acute perturbations in bone turnover in response to exercise across various ages, fitness levels, sexes, and exercise modes. β-CTX-1 is considered an acute and reliable marker of bone resorption. The findings provide robust evidence that exercise disrupts calcium homeostasis, triggered by a decline in iCa and resulting in an increase in PTH and β-CTX-I. The repeatability of the calcium meal's effect on iCa stabilization was confirmed. Methodologically, PTH adj and β-CTX-I adj data required log-transformation due to deviations, but adjustment for hemoconcentration did not alter the interpretation of BTMs, and sweat loss was accounted for as a covariate in β-CTX-I adj analysis, suggesting confidence in these adjusted findings. While 25(OH)D insufficiency was noted in 30% of the sample, the crossover design likely mitigated its impact. Limitations include the focus on elite male athletes and small, clinically insignificant macronutrient differences between interventions.
recommended_alternatives: Further investigation of the timing and nature of exercise sessions on bone turnover
Strategies to attenuate the initial perturbation of blood iCa
Future research could monitor bone formation markers (e.g., procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP)) over days after exercise for longer time courses
Future investigation to identify the optimal dose of preexercise calcium
